lessons.title: Giving opinions
lessons.scenario: Smarty and his friends discuss which film to watch in the club-room.

items.example: As I see it, a comedy is the best.
items.note: Say 'As I see it' at the start of a sentence to share your personal view.

items.example: From my point of view, science is very interesting.
items.note: Use 'From my point of view' to explain how a situation looks to you.

items.example: I strongly believe we should recycle more.
items.note: Say 'I strongly believe' when you feel very sure about your opinion.

items.example: Personally I think summer is better than winter.
items.note: Start with 'Personally I think' to show that this is your own view, not a rule.

items.example: It seems to me that the train is delayed.
items.note: Use 'It seems to me that' to give a polite, gentle opinion based on what you see.

items.example: I feel that everyone should help in the park.
items.note: Say 'I feel that' to share an opinion that comes from your feelings or experience.

grammar.title: Starting a sentence with your opinion
grammar.explanation: Put phrases like As I see it, From my point of view, and Personally I think at the start of your sentence. Use that after It seems to me, I feel, or I strongly believe before a full idea.
examples: As I see it, this book is amazing.
It seems to me that Mia is right.

practice.prompt: Choose the phrase that means 'in my personal view'.
practice.explanation: As I see it introduces your own view on a topic.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: From my point of view, science is very interesting.
practice.answer: From my point of view, science is very interesting.
options: From my point of view, science is very interesting.
From my point of view, history is very boring.
In my opinion, science is very difficult.
practice.explanation: Listen for From my point of view and science is very interesting.

practice.prompt: Match the opinion phrases with their meanings.

pairs.right: From what I see, I think

practice.explanation: I strongly believe shows certainty, It seems to me that is gentle, and Personally I think gives your own view.

practice.prompt: Smarty is very sure about helping nature. Complete his sentence.
practice.text: ___ we should recycle more.
practice.explanation: Use I strongly believe when you have a very firm opinion.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence to share a personal opinion about a film.
practice.answer: Personally I think a comedy is better.
practice.explanation: Start with Personally I think, followed by a comedy is better.

practice.prompt: You see dark clouds outside. Complete the gentle opinion.
practice.text: ___ it is going to rain.
practice.explanation: It seems to me that connects directly to a full clause without a comma.

practice.prompt: Share a warm opinion from your heart. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: ___ everyone should help in the park.
practice.explanation: I feel that takes a full clause right after that.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: From my point of view, a documentary is great.
practice.answer: From my point of view, a documentary is great.
practice.explanation: Practise saying From my point of view smoothly before your opinion.

story.hook: Which film wins the vote in Smarty's room?

image.describe: Inside the cozy club-room, Smarty the black cat stands by a board holding a whistle like a referee while Mia, Sam, and Lily raise their hands to vote on a film.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Welcome to our room! Today I am the referee for our film opinion poll.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: As I see it, a comedy is the best after a long week at school.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: From my point of view, a documentary about the ocean is much better.

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: Personally I think an action film is more exciting.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: I strongly believe we need something fun so everyone can laugh.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It seems to me that we each have a different outlook, Smarty.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: I feel that your belief in good films is great. Let us vote now!

questions.prompt: What kind of film does Mia want to watch?
questions.answer: A comedy
questions.explanation: Mia says: As I see it, a comedy is the best.

questions.prompt: What is Sam's opinion?
questions.answer: A documentary about the ocean is much better.
options: A documentary about the ocean is much better.
An action film is the worst.
questions.explanation: Sam says: From my point of view, a documentary about the ocean is much better.

questions.prompt: How does Lily start her opinion?
questions.answer: Personally I think
questions.explanation: Lily says: Personally I think an action film is more exciting.

mission.setup: Smarty asks for your opinion in the club-room. Answer in your own words.

turns.smarty: We want to watch a film this evening. What do you think?
accept: ^(?:as i see it|personally i think|from my point of view|i feel that|i strongly believe|it seems to me that) (?:a comedy|a cartoon|an action film|a documentary|a horror film) is (?:great|interesting|exciting|better|the best|boring)$
turns.example: Personally I think a comedy is great.
turns.hint: Start with Personally I think or As I see it, then name a film type.

turns.smarty: What about our town park? Should we clean up the litter there?
accept: ^(?:i strongly believe|i feel that|it seems to me that|as i see it|personally i think|from my point of view) (?:we should|everyone should|we must) (?:clean|help|recycle)(?: the park| up the litter| more)?$
turns.example: I strongly believe we should clean the park.
turns.hint: Use I strongly believe or I feel that and say what we should do.

exposure.gloss: a quick vote to see what people think
a person's general view on something
the person who keeps a discussion or game fair
something you strongly think is true

lessons.title: Question tags
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Mia double-check details for the weekend picnic in the club-room.

items.example: It is a sunny day, is not it?
items.note: Add 'is not it?' at the end of a positive 'it is' sentence to check if the listener agrees.

items.example: You like chocolate cake, do not you?
items.note: Use 'do not you?' after a positive 'you' statement to confirm what you think is true.

items.example: Ben did not miss the bus, did he?
items.note: Add 'did he?' after a negative past statement about a boy or man to check the fact.

items.example: They have already bought the tickets, have not they?
items.note: Use 'have not they?' after a positive 'they have' statement to double-check.

items.example: I am on the team, am I not?
items.note: Add 'am I not?' after 'I am' when you want someone to confirm something about you.

items.example: You will not forget the camera, will you?
items.note: Use 'will you?' after 'you will not' to make sure someone remembers a promise.

grammar.title: How question tags work
grammar.explanation: A positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. Match the helper verb (is, do, did, have, will) and the subject pronoun.
examples: It is cold outside, is not it?
He did not call yesterday, did he?

practice.prompt: Complete the question tag for a positive 'It is' sentence.
practice.text: It is a great idea, ___
practice.explanation: It is takes the negative tag is not it?.

practice.prompt: You think Mia likes tea. Check with her.
practice.text: You like hot tea, ___
practice.explanation: A positive present simple statement with you takes do not you?.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: Ben did not miss the bus, did he?
practice.answer: Ben did not miss the bus, did he?
options: Ben did not miss the bus, did he?
Ben missed the bus, did he?
Ben did not miss the bus, will you?
practice.explanation: Because did not miss is negative, the tag is positive: did he?.

practice.prompt: Match the start of each sentence with its question tag.
practice.explanation: Match the verb and subject: have -> have not they?, I am -> am I not?, will not -> will you?.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence to check if Sam and Leo have the snacks.
practice.answer: They have got the snacks, have not they?
practice.explanation: They have takes have not they? at the end.

practice.prompt: Check that you are right. Complete the question.
practice.text: I am right about the time, ___
practice.explanation: After I am, use am I not? to ask for confirmation.

practice.prompt: Remind Sam not to forget the map. Complete the question.
practice.text: You will not forget the map, ___
practice.explanation: You will not takes the positive tag will you?.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: It is a sunny day, is not it?
practice.answer: It is a sunny day, is not it?
practice.explanation: Let your voice rise at the end on is not it? when checking information.

story.hook: Did Ben remember the picnic basket?

image.describe: Smarty and Mia stand by the club-room table checking a picnic list while Sam looks out the window waiting for Ben.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: We are ready for our picnic in the park. Let us double-check everything.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: It is a warm, sunny morning, is not it?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Yes! You like apple juice and sandwiches, do not you?

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Of course! Sam and Leo have already packed the fruit, have not they?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Yes, we have. Ben did not forget the blanket, did he?

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: No, he is coming now. I am helping with the bags, am I not?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Yes, Mia! You will not forget to close the window, will you? Good echo on every reply tag!

questions.prompt: What is the weather like for the picnic?
questions.answer: Warm and sunny
questions.explanation: Mia says: It is a warm, sunny morning, is not it?.

questions.prompt: What did Sam ask about Ben?
questions.answer: If Ben forgot the blanket
questions.explanation: Sam asks: Ben did not forget the blanket, did he?.

questions.prompt: What does Smarty remind Mia to do?
questions.answer: Close the window
questions.explanation: Smarty says: You will not forget to close the window, will you?.

mission.setup: Smarty wants to check some facts with you using question tags.

turns.smarty: Look outside! Tell me it is a nice day and check if I agree.
accept: ^it is a (?:nice|sunny|warm|great|beautiful) day is not it$
turns.example: It is a sunny day, is not it?
turns.hint: Say It is a sunny day, is not it?

turns.smarty: Ask me if I like fish, using a question tag.
accept: ^you like fish do not you$
turns.example: You like fish, do not you?
turns.hint: Say You like fish, do not you?

turns.smarty: Tell me I will not forget my umbrella, and add the tag.
accept: ^you will not forget your umbrella will you$
turns.example: You will not forget your umbrella, will you?
turns.hint: Say You will not forget your umbrella, will you?

exposure.gloss: to check that something is true
to check something a second time
a short question added to the end of a sentence
to repeat the verb from the first part of a sentence

lessons.title: Giving reasons
lessons.scenario: Leo arrives late to the club-room and explains why everyone is delayed.

items.example: I am late, and the reason is that my bus was delayed.
items.note: Say 'the reason is' right before you explain why something happened.

items.example: It was raining hard, and that is why we stayed inside.
items.note: Use 'that is why' after giving a cause to show its result.

items.example: We missed the train because of the traffic jam.
items.note: Put 'because of' before a noun or thing that caused a problem or result.

items.example: The game was cancelled due to the storm.
items.note: Use 'due to' before a noun to give a clear, slightly formal reason.

items.example: Owing to the snow, the school was closed yesterday.
items.note: Say 'owing to' before a noun, often at the start of a sentence, to explain a cause.

items.example: The bridge is broken. For this reason, we must go by boat.
items.note: Start a new sentence with 'For this reason,' to connect a fact to your next action.

grammar.title: Noun after because of, due to, owing to
grammar.explanation: Follow because of, due to, and owing to with a noun phrase like the rain or the traffic jam. Follow the reason is, that is why, and for this reason with a full clause.
examples: We stayed home because of the rain.
It rained. For this reason, we stayed home.

practice.prompt: A noun phrase follows the blank. Choose the right phrase.
practice.text: We were late ___ the traffic jam.
practice.explanation: Use because of before a noun like the traffic jam.

practice.prompt: The first part gives the cause. Connect it to the result.
practice.text: There was a power cut, and ___ the computer is off.
practice.explanation: That is why links a cause to its result clause.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: The game was cancelled due to the storm.
practice.answer: The game was cancelled due to the storm.
options: The game was cancelled due to the storm.
The train was delayed due to the snow.
The game was cancelled because of the rain.
practice.explanation: Listen for cancelled due to the storm.

practice.prompt: Match the two parts of each sentence.

pairs.left: I am tired, and the reason is
The park is closed. For this reason,

practice.explanation: Owing to takes a noun; the reason is and For this reason take full clauses.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence explaining why you are late.
practice.answer: The reason is that my bus was delayed.
practice.explanation: Start with The reason is that, followed by my bus was delayed.

practice.prompt: Start the sentence with a formal reason before the noun.
practice.text: ___ the snow, the station was closed.
practice.explanation: Owing to goes right before a noun phrase like the snow.

practice.prompt: Connect the first sentence to the action in the second sentence.
practice.text: The tap is broken. ___, there is no water.
practice.explanation: For this reason introduces a whole result sentence.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: We missed the train because of the traffic jam.
practice.answer: We missed the train because of the traffic jam.
practice.explanation: Use because of smoothly before the noun phrase the traffic jam.

story.hook: Why did Leo arrive wet and late to the club-room?

image.describe: Leo stands in the club-room doorway holding a wet umbrella while Smarty and Ana look at the rain outside the window.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Hello, Leo! You are very wet and twenty minutes late.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Sorry! I am late, and the reason is that my bus stopped near the bridge.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Was there a traffic jam?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Yes, there was a big traffic jam because of the thunderstorm.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: And the train was cancelled due to the lightning, was it?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Right! Owing to the storm, no trains were running. That is why I walked.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: What a cause and effect! For this reason, let us make hot tea for Leo.

questions.prompt: Why was there a big traffic jam?
questions.answer: Because of the thunderstorm
questions.explanation: Leo says: there was a big traffic jam because of the thunderstorm.

questions.prompt: Why were no trains running?
questions.answer: Owing to the storm
questions.explanation: Leo says: Owing to the storm, no trains were running.

questions.prompt: What does Ana suggest at the end?
questions.answer: Hot tea for Leo
questions.explanation: Ana says: For this reason, let us make hot tea for Leo.

mission.setup: Smarty asks why you were late to the meeting. Give clear reasons.

turns.smarty: You arrived late today! Why did that happen?
accept: ^(?:i am late because of|it happened because of|i was late because of|it was due to) the (?:rain|snow|storm|traffic jam|thunderstorm)$
^the reason is that (?:it was raining|my bus was delayed|i missed the bus)$
turns.example: I was late because of the traffic jam.
turns.hint: Use because of the rain/traffic jam or the reason is that...

turns.smarty: Oh no! What did you do next?
accept: ^that is why i (?:walked|came by bus|came by car|took a taxi)$
^for this reason i (?:walked|came by bus|came by car|took a taxi)$
turns.example: That is why I walked.
turns.hint: Start with That is why I... or For this reason I...

exposure.gloss: the reason you give to make something clear
something that makes another thing happen
a change that happens because of something
what happens at the end because of a cause

lessons.title: Review
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Zara share opinions about town litter, check facts, and explain reasons in the club-room.

practice.prompt: Choose the phrase that introduces your personal view.
practice.explanation: From my point of view shows how you see an issue.

practice.prompt: Check that Zara and Tom have cleaned the park.
practice.text: They have cleaned the park, ___
practice.explanation: They have takes the negative tag have not they?.

practice.prompt: Give a reason before the noun phrase 'air pollution'.
practice.text: Many people are ill ___ air pollution.
practice.explanation: Use due to before a noun phrase like air pollution.

practice.prompt: Match the phrases with their roles in a discussion.
practice.explanation: As I see it shares a view, is not it? checks agreement, and For this reason connects a cause to an action.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence giving a gentle opinion.
practice.answer: It seems to me that litter is a problem.
practice.explanation: It seems to me that introduces a polite, clear opinion.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: You care about nature, do not you?
practice.answer: You care about nature, do not you?
options: You care about nature, do not you?
You care about music, do not you?
They care about nature, have not they?
practice.explanation: You with a positive verb takes do not you?.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: I strongly believe we can solve this problem.
practice.answer: I strongly believe we can solve this problem.
practice.explanation: Practise combining I strongly believe with a clear action.

story.hook: Why is there so much litter near the river?

image.describe: Smarty, Zara, and Tom sit around a table in the club-room looking at a town map with green pins along the river.

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: As I see it, the park near the river is very dirty this week.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: It is full of rubbish, is not it? The reason is that there were many visitors yesterday.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: And there are not enough rubbish bins because of the festival, are there?

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: Right! Owing to many people, the bins were full early. That is why litter is on the grass.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: You want to help clean it up tomorrow, do not you?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: I strongly believe we should! For this reason, let us meet at nine o'clock.

questions.prompt: What is Zara's opinion about the park?
questions.answer: It is very dirty this week.
options: It is very dirty this week.
It is closed due to snow.
questions.explanation: Zara says: As I see it, the park near the river is very dirty this week.

questions.prompt: Why were the bins full early?
questions.answer: Owing to many people
questions.explanation: Zara says: Owing to many people, the bins were full early.

mission.setup: Smarty asks you to share your opinion, check a fact, and give a reason.

turns.smarty: What is your opinion on riding a bicycle to school?
accept: ^(?:as i see it|personally i think|from my point of view|i strongly believe|i feel that) (?:riding a bicycle|a bicycle) is (?:healthy|cheap|great|better|fast|good)$
turns.example: Personally I think a bicycle is healthy.
turns.hint: Use Personally I think or As I see it and describe riding a bicycle.

turns.smarty: Why is a bicycle better than a car in town?
accept: ^(?:the reason is that )?(?:there is no traffic jam|it is cheap|it is healthy)$
^(?:it is good )?because of (?:the traffic jam|air pollution)$
turns.example: It is good because of the traffic jam.
turns.hint: Give a reason with the reason is or because of.

lessons.title: Linking ideas
lessons.scenario: Ana and Tom compare two ideas for the club-room weekend activity.

items.example: The jacket is expensive. However, it is very warm.
items.note: Start a new sentence with 'However,' to introduce a fact that contrasts with your first point.

items.example: Although it was raining, we walked to the park.
items.note: Use 'although' before a full clause to show a surprising contrast between two facts.

items.example: In spite of the cold weather, we played football outside.
items.note: Put 'in spite of' before a noun to show that something happened anyway.

items.example: Even though I was tired, I helped my friend.
items.note: Use 'even though' for a strong contrast, just like 'although' but with extra emphasis.

items.example: Living in town is noisy. On the other hand, everything is near.
items.note: Say 'On the other hand,' when you move to the opposite side of an argument.

items.example: Mia enjoys skiing, whereas Sam prefers swimming.
items.note: Use 'whereas' in the middle of a sentence to compare two opposite facts.

grammar.title: Contrasting clauses vs. nouns
grammar.explanation: Use although, even though, and whereas with a subject and verb. Use in spite of with a noun. Use However and On the other hand at the start of a new sentence.
examples: Although he was ill, he came.
In spite of his cold, he came.

practice.prompt: A noun phrase follows the blank. Choose the right linking phrase.
practice.text: ___ the rain, we had a great picnic.
practice.explanation: In spite of goes before a noun like the rain, while although and even though take a verb.

practice.prompt: Compare Mia and Sam's hobbies in one sentence.
practice.text: Mia likes painting, ___ Sam prefers woodwork.
practice.explanation: Use whereas in the middle of a sentence to contrast two people or things.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: The camera is small. However, it takes amazing photos.
practice.answer: The camera is small. However, it takes amazing photos.
options: The camera is small. However, it takes amazing photos.
The camera is big. However, it is very cheap.
Although the camera is small, it is broken.
practice.explanation: However starts the second sentence to show a positive contrast.

practice.prompt: Match the two halves of each contrasting sentence.

pairs.left: The hotel is cheap. On the other hand,
pairs.right: it is far from the station.

pairs.left: Even though the exam was difficult,

practice.explanation: Match the contrasting ideas logically.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence showing a contrast about the weather.
practice.answer: Although it was cold we went outside.
practice.explanation: Although introduces the clause it was cold before the main clause.

practice.prompt: Add strong emphasis to the contrast. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: ___ he was nervous, Omar spoke clearly on stage.
practice.explanation: Even though goes before a full clause like he was nervous.

practice.prompt: Introduce the opposite side of the argument.
practice.text: Summer is hot. ___, we can swim in the sea.
practice.explanation: On the other hand opens a new sentence with the other side of the topic.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: Mia enjoys skiing, whereas Sam prefers swimming.
practice.answer: Mia enjoys skiing, whereas Sam prefers swimming.
practice.explanation: Pause lightly before whereas when comparing two people.

story.hook: Can Ana and Tom agree on a weekend trip?

image.describe: Ana and Tom sit at the club-room table comparing a mountain trail map and a museum leaflet while Smarty listens carefully.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: I want to hike in the forest tomorrow. However, the forecast says it may rain.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Although the forest is beautiful, a wet trail is dangerous.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: True! On the other hand, the nature reserve is quiet in the rain.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: You love walking outside, whereas I prefer staying dry in the museum.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: What a clear contrast! Even though you want different things, your ideas even out.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: In spite of the cloudy sky, we can visit the museum first and walk if the sun comes out.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Despite my fear of rain, that sounds like a great compromise!

questions.prompt: Why is Tom worried about hiking in the forest?
questions.answer: The trail is dangerous in the rain.
options: The trail is dangerous in the rain.
questions.explanation: Tom says: Although the forest is beautiful, a wet trail is dangerous.

questions.prompt: How does Tom compare himself and Ana?
questions.answer: Ana loves walking outside, whereas Tom prefers the museum.
options: Ana loves walking outside, whereas Tom prefers the museum.
Ana prefers the museum, whereas Tom loves the forest.
questions.explanation: Tom says: You love walking outside, whereas I prefer staying dry in the museum.

mission.setup: Smarty gives you one side of a topic. Add a contrasting idea!

turns.smarty: Our room is quite small. Can you add a positive contrast with However or On the other hand?
accept: ^(?:however|on the other hand) (?:it is|our room is) (?:warm|clean|nice|cozy|great|near|quiet)$
turns.example: However, it is clean.
turns.hint: Start with However or On the other hand, then say something good about the room.

turns.smarty: Compare tea and coffee using whereas.
accept: ^i like tea whereas (?:my friend|sam|mia) likes (?:coffee|latte|juice)$
^tea is hot whereas (?:lemonade|ice|water) is cold$
turns.example: I like tea, whereas Sam likes juice.
turns.hint: Put whereas between two opposite facts.

exposure.gloss: a clear difference between two things
to become balanced or equal
without being stopped by something
in spite of what was just said

lessons.title: Adding points
lessons.scenario: Smarty helps Lily organize her points for a community charity proposal.

items.example: We need drinking water as well as snacks for the trip.
items.note: Use 'as well as' to add one more thing or idea onto something you just mentioned.

items.example: The hotel has a swimming pool. In addition, breakfast is free.
items.note: Start a sentence with 'In addition,' to give an extra supporting point.

items.example: First of all, let us check the agenda.
items.note: Say 'First of all,' to introduce the very first point in a list or discussion.

items.example: Lastly, we must clean the room before we leave.
items.note: Use 'Lastly,' right before your final point so listeners know you are finishing.

items.example: The solar panel saves money. What is more, it is clean.
items.note: Say 'What is more,' when your next point is even stronger or more exciting.

items.example: To begin with, I would like to thank everyone for coming.
items.note: Use 'To begin with,' to open your explanation with your first main idea.

grammar.title: Ordering your points clearly
grammar.explanation: Open with First of all or To begin with. Add extra points with In addition, What is more, or as well as. Close your list with Lastly.
examples: To begin with, the park is dirty. In addition, there is litter near the lake. Lastly, we can clean it together.

practice.prompt: Start the meeting with the very first point.
practice.text: ___, let us look at today's agenda.
practice.explanation: First of all introduces your opening point.

practice.prompt: Add fruit to the shopping list.
practice.text: We bought bread and cheese ___ fresh fruit.
practice.explanation: Use as well as to join an extra noun onto a list.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: The solar panel saves money. What is more, it is clean.
practice.answer: The solar panel saves money. What is more, it is clean.
options: The solar panel saves money. What is more, it is clean.
The solar panel is cheap. Lastly, it is small.
To begin with, the solar panel saves electricity.
practice.explanation: What is more introduces an even stronger second point.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its place in a talk.
practice.explanation: To begin with opens, In addition adds, and Lastly finishes.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence adding an extra benefit.
practice.answer: In addition the workshop is free.
practice.explanation: In addition starts the sentence to add another positive fact.

practice.prompt: Open Lily's proposal with her first point.
practice.text: ___, we want to raise money for the library.
practice.explanation: To begin with introduces the very first point of a talk.

practice.prompt: Finish the list with the final action.
practice.text: ___, we will share the photos online.
practice.explanation: Lastly signals that this is the final point.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: First of all, we need a clear agenda.
practice.answer: First of all, we need a clear agenda.
practice.explanation: Use First of all to organize your ideas from the start.

story.hook: How many points are on Lily's charity list?

image.describe: Lily stands by a flipchart in the club-room pointing to three numbered stars while Smarty and Ben take notes.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Lily, tell us your sequence of ideas for our charity weekend.

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: To begin with, we can bake cakes as well as biscuits to sell at the market.

lines.speaker: Ben

lessons.title: Disagreeing nicely
lessons.scenario: Omar and Mia disagree politely about buying a big screen for the club-room.

items.example: I see your point, but the screen is too expensive.
items.note: Say 'I see your point, but...' to show you understand the other person before sharing a different view.

items.example: I am afraid I disagree with that proposal.
items.note: Use 'I am afraid I disagree' to say no politely without sounding angry.

items.example: I am not convinced that this is the best solution.
items.note: Say 'I am not convinced' when someone's reason has not persuaded you yet.

items.example: That may be true, but we do not have enough money.
items.note: Use 'That may be true, but...' to accept a fact while showing a bigger problem.

items.example: We both have strong views, so let us agree to differ.
items.note: Say 'Let us agree to differ' to end a friendly debate peacefully when neither side changes.

items.example: I take your point about the price, so let us look for a discount.
items.note: Say 'I take your point' to admit that the other speaker made a good argument.

grammar.title: Softening disagreement
grammar.explanation: Soften disagreement by starting with I am afraid or I am not convinced, or by accepting part of the idea first with I see your point, but... or That may be true, but...

lessons.title: Choosing
lessons.scenario: Smarty and his friends choose between a forest picnic and a museum visit.

items.example: Shall we go for the picnic in the park?
items.note: Ask 'Shall we go for...?' to suggest choosing one specific thing together.

items.example: I would prefer to visit the museum because it is cloudy.
items.note: Say 'I would prefer...' to tell the group which choice you like more.

items.example: Let us take the direct train so we are on time.
items.note: Use 'Let us take...' when picking an action, route, or item together.

items.example: If it rains, we could always go to the cinema.
items.note: Say 'We could always...' to offer an easy backup idea.

items.example: How about meeting at half past two?
items.note: Ask 'How about...?' followed by a noun or -ing verb to make a friendly suggestion.

items.example: Both films look great, so it is a toss-up between them.
items.note: Say 'It is a toss-up' when two choices seem equally good and hard to pick between.

grammar.explanation: Use Shall we go for + noun, How about + noun or -ing verb, and We could always + base verb to suggest ideas. Use I would prefer to state your choice.

lessons.title: Summing up

mission.setup: Take part in the final debate with Smarty! Give an opinion, disagree politely, choose, and sum up.

turns.smarty: First, give your opinion on planting trees in the park.
accept: ^(?:as i see it|personally i think|from my point of view|i strongly believe|i feel that) (?:planting trees|trees) (?:is|are) (?:great|a benefit|healthy|good|worth it)$
turns.example: Personally I think planting trees is a benefit.
turns.hint: Start with Personally I think or As I see it and share your view.

turns.smarty: Some people say planting trees takes too much time. Disagree politely!
accept: ^(?:i see your point but|that may be true but|i am afraid i disagree|i am not convinced) (?:it is worth it|trees are a benefit|we can work in a team)$
turns.example: That may be true, but it is worth it.
turns.hint: Use That may be true, but... or I see your point, but... and say it is worth it.

turns.smarty: Now suggest choosing the park project together!
accept: ^shall we go for (?:the park|planting trees)$
^i would prefer (?:the park|to plant trees)$
turns.example: Shall we go for the park?
turns.hint: Ask Shall we go for the park? or say I would prefer the park.

turns.smarty: Close the debate with a short summary!
accept: ^(?:to sum up|in conclusion|all in all|to put it briefly) (?:we will help our town|it is a great decision|the main point is that we work together|it is worth it)$
turns.example: To sum up, we will help our town.
turns.hint: Start with To sum up or In conclusion and finish strongly.

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: All in all, that was our best debate, was not it?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat stretches happily in the sunlit club-room after the meeting.

panels.speaker: Mia
panels.text: Yes, it was! The main point is that we start cleaning the park on Saturday.

panels.speaker: Sam
panels.text: Wait a minute! Look behind the filing cabinet. There is a small black box!

image.describe: Sam points behind an old metal filing cabinet in the corner of the club-room where a dusty black box sits.

panels.speaker: Omar
panels.text: It has a heavy lock on it. I am not convinced we can open it.

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: However, I found a spare key in my desk last week. Let us try!

panels.speaker: Ana
panels.text: In spite of the old lock, the key turns! Look inside the box!

image.describe: Smarty opens the small black box on the club-room table, revealing a faded paper map and a shining ancient coin.

panels.speaker: Mia
panels.text: There is a faded map and an ancient coin from the old fortress!

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: As I see it, a brand-new adventure is about to begin!

image.describe: Smarty and his friends gather closely around the faded fortress map with excited, curious faces.
